claims.text: At ambient temperature, HEA-coating tribological performance is governed primarily by microstructural complexity and hardness rather than thermally activated mechanisms.
Enhanced configurational entropy can stabilize single-phase high-entropy alloys.
At ambient temperature, high configurational entropy prevents phase decomposition of the HEA coating.
The HEA coating forms a protective oxide or mechanically mixed tribolayer during ambient dry sliding.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the protective tribolayer.
The protective tribolayer retards adhesive wear and abrasive ploughing.
Thermal softening or oxidation dominates wear in high-temperature regimes.
High coating hardness resists abrasive ploughing.
A ductile matrix prevents brittle fracture of the coating during wear.
An FCC/BCC multiphase microstructure with intermetallic precipitates produces high hardness and strain-hardening capability.
HEA coatings with a balanced multiphase microstructure will have low, relatively constant wear rates at ambient temperature.
Wear resistance is expected to increase linearly with hardness.
Brittle phases can cause deviations from the hardness–wear-resistance relationship.
A high volume fraction of hard, Ti-rich intermetallic phases may lower wear relative to a single-phase FCC coating if toughness is sufficient to prevent spalling.
Excessive brittle-intermetallic content causes abrasive fracture and delamination.
Insufficient hardness permits plastic deformation and material transfer, resulting in severe adhesive wear.
Wear rate will increase sharply when coating hardness falls below approximately 500 HV.
Wear rate will increase sharply when brittle phases exceed 30% by volume.
Performance degrades significantly when coating hardness is below 400 HV.
Flash temperatures above 200 °C shift the wear mechanism toward thermal softening and degrade wear resistance.

contradictions.description: The proposed hardness boundary is inconsistent or at least unresolved: degradation is predicted below approximately 500 HV in one field but below 400 HV in the boundary field.

The predicted outcome allows a high fraction of hard intermetallics to improve wear resistance when toughness prevents spalling, whereas the boundary categorically assigns degradation to brittle-intermetallic fractions above 30%.

The falsification rule treats lowest wear with no delamination in the intermetallic-rich coating as falsifying, although the predicted outcome already permits that result when toughness is sufficient.
